title: Is anyone creating their own Physics engine?
author: Dangerous_Three_8506
selftext:
I can't decide if I should use Godot or make my own. I don't care for the companies looking for royaltys from soon to be outdated software.

The internet will tell you to use Godot, but I am wondering if anyone took a leap of faith and said nah, AI is awesome. Lets accelerate and get the physics engine proof done for everyone to see.

Gemini acts like its an expert in how to use AI for game development. Its really foolish.

comments.author: Nomski88
comments.body: I'm building my own custom game engine loosely based around quakes design but with my own improvements. I specifically designed it to support lightweight rigid physics systems as a later development milestone while I work through the core development. The goal is to have basic kinematic physics for a simple FPS engine but with support for things like objects falling and rolling around a level or basic rag doll physics.

replies.author: Dangerous_Three_8506
replies.body: Is your project a ground zero project? Never existed before AI?

replies.author: Nomski88
replies.body: No, I'm using a local coding agent. I'm about three weeks into development.

comments.author: Old-Entertainment844
comments.body: Yeah, currently working on a physics engine. Early stages yet since my game only needs it for collision right now but I aim to expand it for future projects.

replies.author: Dangerous_Three_8506
replies.body:
Are you doing object collision and event collision? 
If you had a village are all the villagers colliding with the village or are you only doing collison like a foot kicking a ball?

I just started researching today. I was doing my own map editor, blender, first steps of the game. Today marks advanced physics day 1.

replies.author: Old-Entertainment844
replies.body:
Objects and events, the same underlying math also resolves combat damage. 

Main benefit is that it's extremely lightweight so that there can be hundreds of interactions per frame on dogshit hardware, since I'm currently limited to dogshit hardware.

comments.author: PyreForgedev
comments.body: I've been working on one for a year or so now (PyreForge.dev)but have gotten bit hard by scope, getting closer and closer to finished thankfully.

comments.author: rpstudios_mx
comments.body:
Gemini relies heavily on the instructions you give it, and its long-term memory is terrible; however, it excels at handling short, highly specific tasks using the knowledge you provide.



As for the physics engine, it always depends on what you're developing and the intended use case; deciding whether the time investment is worth it for you and your projects is a noble pursuit, though mere mortals like me will just stick to Godot's default options, haha.

replies.author: SnuffleBag
replies.body: When you say 'excels', have you actually tried the other frontier models for comparison? Gemini is barely in the top 10.

comments.author: Melodic-Chemistry127
comments.body: I'm building a full AI-first authoring toolkit, including a game engine. I will be either using a third party solution or rolling my own - I'm pretty undecided. I'd be curious to hear what direction you'll end up choosing.

comments.author: __SlimeQ__
comments.body:
godot is not a physics engine, it uses one, which can be easily replaced

if you're using gemini for gamedev right now you're a solid year behind on progress. the meta right now is opus 5.5

I'd recommend learning more about the problems you're trying to solve and what other people have already contributed before you just shoot for the stars for no reason

replies.author: CrashNowhereDrive
replies.body: This is what's going to save us from the slopocalypse.  Humans getting dumber faster than AI gets smarter.

comments.author: Neither_Berry_100
comments.body:
I created my own game engine in Java using the lwjgl (opengl and openal) years ago without ai. More like a framework than engine but whatever.

It lacked advanced stuff like great lighting and collision detection for complex shapes. I never got my model importer working 100%. My rotation system was kind of broken but I made due and made it work.

The basics worked really well and my work flow was good. But there was quite a bit of code. Probably 20k or a little more for the reusable code.

I'm using Unity these days.

comments.author: japherwocky
comments.body: I had Opus work out an IK system and it was a one or two shot affair, I think you probably could.  I wanted to add that prototyping in a browser / three.js is warp speed compared to working with godot or unreal, etc.  try just hacking it out in your browser first, and then think about switching to a more mature engine, imo

replies.author: FutureLynx_
replies.body: three.js is faster than godot at producing games with ai?

replies.author: japherwocky
replies.body: I haven't personally tried godot, but yes I was very surprised, because you can use a browser MCP the agent can do a lot of QA by looking at the browser and setting debug points.  I took a project I'd been hacking on in UE5 and development is much faster and easier in three.js.

replies.author: FutureLynx_
replies.body: Yeah unreal is very slow with AI. But i thought between Godot and Three.js, that Godot would be better, give or take.

comments.author: CC_NHS
comments.body:
if you want to build your own physics engine with AI, I am sure it can put something together that works. but let's be realistic in expectations. anything opus 5.5 does off a prompt won't be on the level of Havok, PhysX, Chaos or Unity DOTS physics. If you are a physics programmer yourself it can probably get you there, but Opus alone won't.

I did build my own about 15 years ago. Based of bounding boxes. It was not great but it worked. Took me three months, it was a learning experience, existing solutions from Unity and Unreal were obviously way better, but that was not the point. :)

Opus will be able to build an entire engine I am sure. But it won't be competitive, it will be a learning project or demo type thing.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: Not from scratch, but combined a few libraries and make something bespoke.

comments.author: Square-Yam-3772
comments.body:
you are spending extra time if your project doesn't justify a custom game engine

using an existing engine is also good if you want help i.e. you can google "XYZ in godot" 

you are on your own if you use your custom engine. 

it doesn't take a leap of faith or anything. its just time/token vs rewards

comments.author: kytheon
comments.body: If you can't make a game, don't start by making a physics engine, lol.

comments.author: Weekly_Raise_781
comments.body: I had frontier models create networked custom physics for non euclidean portal engine and they can do the job well. Design it with ai for your use case, choose suitable iterator and scene complexity early on.

comments.author: SnuffleBag
comments.body:
Companies looking for royalties.. from an open source engine?

There's half a dozen competent open source physics engines in the world, it's probably the component that should worry you the least.

comments.author: CycleMother2006
comments.body:
You can build your own. Opus is good enough. Even dumbed down Astra.

However it will probably take a week or so of max usage to get it into a workable state and cover a fair number of things you'd generally expect in a barebone physics engine. That's not the problem though. The problem is just that you WILL undoubtedly experience issues in perpetuity as you use the thing and have to patch and debug them one by one as you go. And then it's not just physics you'd be building from scratch, you'd have to do basic things like character controllers, animation handling, particle/vfx systems, etc. All of it needs building, all of it needs optimizing, all of it needs profilers and debuggers.

You can do it, but you will spend the next ?year? getting it to the same point you could've just had with some other engine. Now if you want to do it because you intend to learn this custom engine you're building and you'll know each piece as it gets put in intimately, so that you'll be able to use it properly and see workflow benefits from it long-term, and only ever intend to build a very specific kind of game that this engine is addressing.. Then sure, there might be a real use case for you doing so. I personally was tempted down that road just because I would've loved an engine that had nothing extraneous in it, that was specifically something I knew well the ins and outs of, because I hate working in environments with 12,000 buttons that I'll never use. However I knew it'd distract me from my actual projects and become an excuse to work on something else.

Honestly though... Give it a try for a week or two. See how far you get in that time building the engine. And try to get a feel for the pitfalls you might face and the commitment you're asking of yourself as well as any benefits you see with your workflow from doing it. Then make a decision.

comments.author: akanas
comments.body: So... create your own physics engine using AI which AI won't know how to effectively make use of? What's the point?

comments.author: Cute-Wonder-5317
comments.body:
I started doing something similar a while ago. At first, I also thought I was unnecessarily complicating things, but getting into collisions, gravity, integration, and contact resolution is quite interesting.

I don't know if it will ever become a "complete" engine, but as a project to understand what's happening behind those abstractions, it makes a lot of sense.
